title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Substantive prompts

I am creating a regression case study in R and Quarto. My question is “How do race, distance, and gender affect race walking speed?” The response is speed and the main predictors are distance, gender, and interaction between distance and gender. Also, my course-based core model is multiple-linear regression. My main result so far is woman have a predicted average race-walking speed of 29.76 meters/minute lower than men. I found this limitation: race distance and gender don’t fully account for speed as there are underlying factors and covariates such as race-walking experience and age. Suggest three feasible extensions that keep the core analysis connected to regression methods taught in my class. One option may be a model not taught in class used as a comparator. For each, explain how it strengthens the same research question, how its result would enter the final case study, the implementation steps, and two ways I could verify it. Do not choose for me.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
My decisions

Accepted: I used the suggestion to test whether the relationship with distance is curved so we can fit the data better and change the estimated gender difference at different distances.
Changed: Although we had the limitation about distance and gender not being able to fully account for speed and look at other variables like age and experience, there is nothing for those variables in this dataset. Therefore, we will have to forego that suggestion.
Rejected or corrected: Similar to the response above, the advice to add age and race-walking experience is unsuitable since we don’t have data on those two variables.

Connection to the final case study: Identify where the extension’s method and result appear on the final page and how they strengthen the course-based analysis.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Independent verification

Check and result: I compared the linear and quadratic models using anova(). The comparison showed 0 added degrees of freedom and an RSS difference of about 1.46e-11. This comparison did not show that the quadratic model improved fit.
Check and result: I compared the linear and quadratic models using 10-fold cross-validation. Both had an RMSE of 13.90408m/min, so the quadratic model did not reduce prediction error compared with the linear model on these folds.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Remaining limitation
One important limitation is that an F-test couldn’t be calculated because the quadratic model added zero estimable parameters compared with the linear model. This is likely because distance only has two distinct values and with that, the squared-distance term can be redundant with the intercept and linear-distance terms, so it adds no new information.

title: Race Walking
text:
The question
Competitive race walking was first introduced a few centuries ago in England. Its expansion interested us in finding how race distance and gender effect race walking speed. For this analysis, our target audience is competitive race walkers. Our hope is to help these racers optimize their racing times and speeds.
The data were gathered by the World Athletics Race Walking Team Championships. The full datset can be found outline through the following URL: https://data.scorenetwork.org/walking/racewalking_10k_20k_speeds_2024.html
Important variables in this dataset include gender, distance, and walking speed for each observational unit, the individual racer. These predictors enable us to recognize the relationships between each predictor and the response.

title: Race Walking
text:
What the baseline shows
We will use the multiple linear regression model because we have two or more variables (race distance and gender) to predict the outcome of our continuous response variable (speed). This model will allow us to see how the variables independently affect the outcome before adding the interaction.
Holding race distance constant, women have a predicted average race-walking speed of 27.96 meters/minute lower than men. One specific limitation is that race distance and gender don’t fully account for speed as there are underlying factors and covariates such as race-walking experience and age.

baseline <- lm(SPEED ~ DISTANCE + GENDER, data = racewalking)
